GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and this picture builds a staircase of more equal sides up to its top corner.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Slide the angle control to try David's question, or press Reset to start again.
45°
Look for the math

The puzzle asks for the apex angle of an isosceles triangle that allows a chain of equal sides. David Radcliffe's question had one answer, 45°, but the applet shows that the same chain works for nearly every angle below 60°.

A staircase of equal sides

Start with AB = AC and base BC. Put D on the right side so that BD = BC (two ticks in the picture). Put E on the left side on the perpendicular bisector of BD, so BE = DE (one tick). The applet then uses that same length twice more: EF = DE and AF = EF. The logic test checks all four equalities for 238 angles below 60° and for 300 random angles: they hold everywhere except a tiny gap just above 45°, where the circle at E misses the line and the applet simply puts F on top of D.

Angle chasing

Write A for the apex angle. Chasing the equal angles around the four triangles gives

BCD: A, 90 − A/2, 90 − A/2
BDE: 90 − 3A/2, 90 − 3A/2, 3A
DEF: 2A, 180 − 4A, 2A
AEF: A, A, 180 − 2A

These are the article's formulas (with B and C swapped to match the picture). The logic test compares them with the measured angles at every quarter degree under 60°. Above 45° the middle triangle turns over, so its base angles become 180 − 2A and its third angle 4A − 180; the test uses those values there.

When is it really a decomposition?

For A < 45° the four triangles BCD, BDE, DEF and AEF fit together exactly: their areas add up to the area of the whole triangle. At A = 45° the points D and F coincide, leaving just three triangles. Between 45° and 60° the equal sides still match, but F lies past D, so the lines cross and the areas no longer add up. At 60° the chain collapses onto the apex; beyond that it stops at the base. Try the slider at 30°, 45° and 55° to see all three cases.

Two pairs of similar triangles

Using the angle table, the pair BDE, AEF is similar when 180 − 2A = 3A, and the pair BCD, DEF is similar when 180 − 4A = A. Both equations give A = 36°, the golden triangle. The article also says that CDE and AEF are the two obtuse triangles while BCD and DEF are acute; angle chasing shows that sentence is true only for 30° < A < 45°. Outside that window a different triangle is obtuse, and the logic test checks the exact window.

Press the 36° button and compare the two pairs of triangles: each pair has the same three angles, even though the triangles have different sizes.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
